_note: BLOCK-LEVEL markdown (A4) — the `<markdown>` element. This is the twin of, not a replacement for, `<text markdown="true">`: that one renders the INLINE intents only (emphasis, code, links) because SwiftUI's Text collapses block intents, and it stays exactly as it was. `<markdown>` is the block vocabulary a README needs — headings, paragraphs, lists, fenced code, blockquotes, tables, images, rules. Cases are (source → a neutral block tree) with no host types in them, so the Kotlin and Swift renderers implement the same file rather than a description of it. INLINE content inside a block is NOT re-specified here: each block carries its raw inline source and every renderer feeds it to the inline parser this corpus's sibling already pins.
_safety: Every case that could inject markup is here on purpose. No renderer may reach innerHTML: the DOM side constructs nodes and the SSR side escapes every run, so an authored or BOUND document is structurally incapable of injecting script. Link and image targets ride the same http/https/mailto/tel/relative allowlist the inline parser uses; a refused target renders as text, never as a live navigation the author did not write.

limits._why: A markdown document here is a package README — authored copy or fetched data. Each bound caps a different allocation axis, and the remainder past a bound renders as plain text rather than throwing.

cases.name: a-soft-wrap-stays-one-paragraph
cases._why: Hard-wrapped prose is the normal shape of a README; treating each line as a block would double-space every document.

cases.name: a-hash-with-no-space-is-not-a-heading
cases._why: `#hashtag` is ordinary prose and must survive as such.

cases.name: a-wrapped-list-item-stays-one-item
cases._why: The CommonMark lazy-continuation law, and the F7 defect: a plain line after a list item is that item's own paragraph continuing, not a new block. Hard-wrapped items are the normal shape of authored docs; splitting them double-renders every wrapped bullet.

cases.name: an-indented-continuation-stays-in-its-item
cases._why: The indented spelling of the same law: continuation lines aligned under the item content are the common editor-wrap shape.

cases.name: a-lazy-line-continues-the-deepest-item
cases._why: Laziness attaches to the INNERMOST open paragraph, so an unindented wrap after a nested item continues that nested item.

cases.name: a-fence-interrupts-a-list-item
cases._why: The boundary of laziness: a line that OPENS a block is never a continuation. Fence, heading, rule, quote, table and image each pin one branch of the shared block-start predicate.

cases.name: a-blockquote-continues-lazily
cases._why: The same law on the quote container: an unmarked paragraph line keeps the quote open.

cases.name: only-a-paragraph-continues-a-quote-lazily
cases._why: Laziness is a PARAGRAPH law: when the quote's innermost open block is not a paragraph (a heading here), the unmarked line falls outside the quote.

cases.name: fenced-code-keeps-its-language-and-its-bytes
cases._why: Code is the one place markdown must NOT interpret anything: the asterisks and underscores inside a fence are code, and a renderer that runs the inline parser over them corrupts the sample.

cases.name: an-unterminated-fence-still-closes-at-the-end
cases._why: A truncated document must render, not swallow the rest of the page.

cases.name: a-ragged-table-row-is-padded-rather-than-dropped
cases._why: A row short of cells is an authoring slip in a README; dropping it silently loses content the author wrote.

cases.name: an-image-with-a-refused-scheme-renders-as-TEXT
cases._why: The XSS pin. A refused target never becomes a live element; the author's label survives as prose so nothing silently disappears.

cases.name: raw-html-in-the-source-is-TEXT-not-markup
cases._why: The other XSS pin, and the reason no renderer may reach innerHTML. A README fetched from a registry is untrusted input.

cases.name: a-realistic-readme-fragment
cases._why: The composition case: every block kind adjacent to every other, which is where a line-oriented parser's state machine actually breaks.
